content.title: What is Input and Output in Java?
content.description: Input refers to receiving data from the user or another source, while output refers to displaying or sending processed information. Java provides several classes for handling input and output, with Scanner being the most commonly used for console input.

content.content: Every interactive Java application requires a way to accept data from users and display results. Java uses the Scanner class to read input from the keyboard and the System.out object to print output to the console.

content.title: Why Learn Scanner?
content.content: Scanner is one of the first Java classes every programmer learns because almost every beginner program accepts user input.
Java provides multiple methods for displaying output on the console. The most commonly used methods are print(), println(), and printf().

items.question: print()
items.answer: Displays text without moving to the next line.

items.question: println()
items.answer: Displays text and moves the cursor to the next line.

items.question: printf()
items.answer: Displays formatted output similar to the C programming language.

content.content: The Scanner class belongs to the java.util package. Before using it, the package must be imported and a Scanner object must be created.

content.title: Creating a Scanner Object
content.code:
import java.util.Scanner;

Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);

content.content: Scanner provides different methods for reading different kinds of data such as integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and boolean values.

content.title: Reading User Input

content.content: A Scanner object can read multiple values one after another. Each input is stored in an appropriate variable according to its data type.

content.title: Reading Multiple Values

content.content: Many beginners confuse next() and nextLine(). The difference is that next() reads only one word, while nextLine() reads the complete line including spaces.

content.title: Common Interview Question
content.content: The difference between next() and nextLine() is one of the most frequently asked Java interview questions for beginners.
After reading input, it is good practice to close the Scanner object to release system resources.

content.title: Closing Scanner
Taking an Order at a Restaurant
content.content: Imagine a waiter taking your order. You provide the information (input), the waiter writes it down (Scanner), and later serves the prepared food (output).

content.title: Interview Importance
content.content: Interviewers often ask how Scanner works, the difference between next() and nextLine(), and how to read different data types from the console.

items.question: Why do we import Scanner?
items.answer: Because Scanner belongs to the java.util package and is not available automatically.

items.question: Why does nextLine() sometimes skip input?
items.answer: Because nextInt(), nextDouble(), and similar methods leave the newline character in the input buffer.

items.question: Why should Scanner be closed?
items.answer: Closing Scanner releases system resources and follows good programming practices.

content.title: Remember This
content.description: Use next() for a single word, nextLine() for a complete sentence, and always import java.util.Scanner before creating a Scanner object.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: System.out.print(), println(), and printf() display output.
Scanner reads user input from the keyboard.
next() reads one word while nextLine() reads an entire line.
Always close the Scanner object after use.
